_meta.baseline_commit: signalvsnoise-v8 (owner-supplied researched rebuild: web-search pre-pass + cited synthesis)
_meta.v5_note: v4's regex (CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE) was verb-conjugation-specific ('evidence shows/suggests/supports') and missed 12 of 13 real violations in the very next live test, a parenting/screen-time topic: 'the evidence tends to show,' 'observational research,' 'reviews of homework research... broadly recognized in ... literature,' 'researchers argue,' 'is associated with,' 'historically,' 'documented,' 'the evidence on X is Y.' Narrow verb-matching does not generalize across the many ways a model phrases 'I reviewed a body of evidence' — v5's list is now broad WORD/PHRASE matching (evidence/research + up to 3 words + a wide verb set, bare 'literature'/'historically'/'documented'/'associated with', etc.), verified against all 13 new violations plus 7 legitimate ALLOWED sentences (0 false positives, 0 false negatives) before shipping. ARCHITECTURE CHANGE: enforcement moved from a whole-CALL regenerate (v4) to PER-FIELD regenerate (v5) — enforceClaimModeFields()/regenerateField()/setAtPath() rewrite only the flagged sentence (cheap, MODELS.FAST, no JSON schema to fill), preserving everything the model got right instead of risking a whole-half regenerate trading one violation for a different one elsewhere. A field that still fails after its one regeneration attempt is left as-is and the EXISTING structural clean()-filter (unchanged) drops the enclosing item, same fallback as before. NEW: a traceability/scope-creep guard (rule 21 extended + 5 new outputGuard entries) — the same live test also introduced 'free-range parenting' and invented 'the core of free-range parenting' as a model-generated definition, neither of which the visitor raised (visitor supplied only screen time, tiger vs. free-range as a *label pair*, and homework — not a definition of any of them). Rule 21 now states an explicit traceability test (A: a supplied claim, B: a necessary distinction, C: an examined source — if none apply, don't write it). Also reinforced: rule 26 (new) — the_signal doesn't need one item per noise item, don't insert an unprompted epistemic lesson (e.g. 'before-and-after comparisons') the visitor didn't raise, don't invent an individual child/person to apply a population claim to (that belongs in what_general_claims_cant_decide, not the general bottom line). UI: a 'CLAIM ANALYSIS' mode badge with a tooltip now renders under ANALYZING (source_analysis/verified_research labels are unreachable today — this tool performs no live retrieval — and are not yet built; add them only if that capability is ever added). Catalog copy (src/data/tools.js description/seoDescription/primer.get) and svn_tagline reworded away from 'stronger evidence'/'genuinely unsettled' framing that implied the tool always has access to an evidence base, per the same principle as SOURCE MODE. Live-tested against the exact parenting/screen-time/homework scenario (0 banned-phrase hits, 0 field-fix regenerations needed — the strengthened prompt got it right without needing the backstop this time; the backstop's correctness was verified separately via 20 unit test cases against the regex directly). DO NOT revert to whole-call regeneration or narrow the banned-phrase list back to verb-conjugation matching — both were the specific gaps this pass closed.
_meta.v4_note: A THIRD 'final corrections' pass, same day as v3, found the identical literature-review-voice failure in a domain not yet tested — finance ('persistent tracking of fund returns... across multiple markets and asset classes,' 'the evidence covers funds that survived long enough to be measured,' a fabricated survivorship-bias limitation for a dataset never examined). Three prompt-only passes had not fully suppressed this, so v4 adds what they didn't have: a deterministic, ENGLISH-ONLY code-level backstop (see signal-vs-noise.js's CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE / findBannedPhrase / callClaimModeChecked) — every prose field is scanned against a fixed phrase list, a violating half is regenerated once with the exact offending phrase quoted back at it, and any array item that still violates after that is silently dropped rather than shown. The prompt still tries hard to get it right the first time (extensive new PERSONALITY rules, worked BAD/GOOD examples for the fee/valuation/real-estate/survivorship/professional-referral/ranking-against-unnamed-alternatives failures) — the regex is the guarantee, not a replacement for it. SCHEMA CHANGE: genuinely_debated (with nullable what_supports_one_view/another_view, introduced in v3) is REMOVED entirely and replaced by two separate top-level arrays: still_worth_verifying[] ({question, why_it_matters, what_would_help} — a genuinely unresolved GENERAL empirical question, never a fabricated two-sided debate) and what_general_claims_cant_decide[] (plain strings — person-specific questions a general analysis can never resolve, e.g. 'whether direct real estate fits your actual situation'). v3's null-views mechanism for person-dependent questions is superseded by this split, not extended. Response also gains analysis_mode ('claim_analysis', hard-locked in code, not model-self-reported) and sources_examined (always [] today — no source-paste feature exists). Caps changed: the_signal 4->3, still_worth_verifying capped at 2 (was genuinely_debated at 3), what_general_claims_cant_decide capped at 3, the_bottom_line.what_would_change_the_answer 2->3. i18n: svn_nuance reworded 'Limits:' -> "What it doesn't establish:"; svn_debated_header reworded 'Still Unsettled' -> 'Still Worth Verifying'; new keys svn_verify_why/svn_verify_would_help/svn_cant_decide_header; svn_one_view/svn_another_view/svn_why_unsettled are now orphaned (left in the locale files, no longer referenced in JSX — the two-sided-debate UI was removed, not relabeled). outputGuard.prohibit grew from 28 to 37 entries. DO NOT reverse the schema split or the code-level regex backstop — three prompt-only passes already proved insufficient on their own.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden signal-vs-noise). v2 (2026-09-09) fixed the health-domain instances of the tool implying a literature review it never performed. v3 (2026-09-10) fixed the SAME failure mode recurring in a non-health (career/labor) domain — 'wage data shows,' an invented MBA-recruiting market map, an invented causal mechanism for job-switching pay, a strawmanned 'follow your passion' critique, an extra unrequested career-advice claim, two noise_type mislabels, an unsupported publicity/selection-bias claim used to rebut an overclaim with another overclaim, debate-club phrasing, and a STILL UNSETTLED section forced into a two-sided-evidence shape it didn't have for a person-dependent question. v4 (same day) is documented in v4_note above. v5 (2026-09-10) is documented in v5_note above. v6 (2026-09-10) is documented in v6_note above.
_meta.prior_notes: v2 (2026-09-09) was a full owner-supplied rewrite: the v1 tool asserted "real consensus," named specific actors as "generating noise," and invoked specific research designs, biomarkers, genetic variants, and validation findings from memory as though it had performed a sourced evidence review — exactly the authority the tool was never in a position to claim. Schema changed completely from v1 (why_this_field_is_noisy -> framing; the_signal.items[].why_we_know_this -> basis; .the_nuance -> limits; genuinely_debated[].side_a/side_b -> what_supports_one_view/what_supports_another_view (later removed entirely in v4); the_noise[] gained what_the_evidence_supports_instead alongside renamed what_went_wrong (was the_problem); the_bottom_line's three single-string fields became three arrays; sources_of_noise[].actor/incentive/how_to_spot_it -> source_type/how_it_distorts/how_to_recognize_it, no longer naming an accused actor). Guards added that pass: NO_QUOTE_RULE, router.outputStandard='v2' + outputGuard, and a post-guard structural validation pass (see code comment: the guard mutates its argument in place and its repair pass can leave a field incomplete despite instructions not to).
_meta.v6_note: A FOURTH 'final corrections' pass, sleep domain, confirmed the deterministic claim_analysis mode switch (v4) had finally killed the fake-literature-review voice, but found a narrower, different failure: unlabeled empirical premises imported from memory that never use evidence-provenance wording at all, so CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE cannot catch them ('most adults need roughly 7-9 hours', 'light exposure is one input to the body's circadian timing system', 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness'), plus a logical non-sequitur reasoning backward from a metaphor's usefulness to a fact about the thing it describes ('if a single recovery night fully erased all sleep debt, the metaphor wouldn't be useful'), plus a bottom line that broke back into sleep/parenting/finance guidance and invented personal context nobody supplied in what_would_change_the_answer. FIX (prompt-level, not regex — this class of error has no stable lexical marker a regex can key on): new rule 27 ('WHAT AUTHORIZES THIS SENTENCE?') gives the model an explicit 3-way test before writing any factual sentence — A. USER_CLAIM (the visitor supplied it), B. LOGIC (follows from the claim's own structure, no empirical finding needed), C. LABELED_BACKGROUND (genuinely ordinary vocabulary-only background, used sparingly, never the central empirical answer) — rewrite or remove if none apply. New rule 28 fixes the metaphor non-sequitur (critique what a metaphor fails to establish, never reason backward from 'what would make it useful'). New rule 29 locks the bottom line to summarizing the claim analysis only, and reserves personal-situation language in what_would_change_the_answer for when the visitor actually supplied enough personal context to identify a real gap. NORTH STAR gained a prepended 3-line frame: use knowledge to understand the claim, logic to test it, evidence to settle it. TRAP HIT AND FIXED DURING THIS PASS: the rule 27/29 illustrative BAD examples quoted the exact attractor phrase 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness' TWICE, verbatim — live testing showed the model echoing that near-verbatim phrase straight into output (a known trap: worked BAD-example text gets copied rather than avoided, see deftbrain-voice-prompt-traps memory). Fixed by rewriting both examples to describe the ERROR PATTERN in the abstract (no specific number, no specific mechanism, no specific magnitude-of-benefit claim to copy) plus an explicit 'this is illustrating a pattern, not a script — a close paraphrase is the same violation' instruction. Verified 0 banned-phrase / 0 attractor-phrase hits across 3 consecutive live regenerations of the exact sleep scenario after the reword (the run before the reword produced the attractor phrase; the runs after did not). UI: added a visible 'No outside sources reviewed' sub-label beside the CLAIM ANALYSIS badge (the existing badge only had it in a hover tooltip, poor discoverability) and a 'Research These Claims' disclosure at the end of results, built from still_worth_verifying (falling back to what_would_change_the_answer) with one external search-engine link per open question — pure frontend, no new backend capability. This is deliberately NOT a live-retrieval / verified-research mode: the tool has no wired search or fetch capability, and building real retrieval is an infrastructure decision (external dependency, cost per request, latency, reliability) flagged to the owner rather than silently built or silently dropped, same position as the v5 note. i18n: svn_honest_uncertainty relabeled '? What Could Change the Answer' -> '? What Would Help' across all 13 languages (claim-analysis mode is never about the visitor's personal situation, so the more evidence-focused label is now the default; a personalized 'what could change the answer' framing would need a genuinely supplied personal-context case, which this tool does not yet branch on). New keys: svn_no_sources_reviewed, svn_research_these_claims, svn_research_intro, svn_search_this (13 languages each). DO NOT re-quote a specific number, mechanism, or magnitude figure in rule 27/28/29's illustrative examples — describe the pattern, never the sentence.
_meta.v7_note: V7 replaces 'regex + one regen' with a five-stage CLAIM ANALYSIS VALIDATION PIPELINE in the route: (1) CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, demoted to cheap first-pass detection; (2) a SEMANTIC EMPIRICAL-RESOLUTION CHECK — a judged call asking ONE narrow question per field (does this text assert or rely on a real-world proposition that was not supplied, not sourced in this run, and materially helps decide the claim? hedges do not convert FAIL to PASS); (3) one per-field REWRITE with the owner's exact rewrite prompt; (4) REVALIDATE the rewrite alone (regex + judge, batch size 1); (5) a fixed, LOCALIZED SAFE FALLBACK per field type (13 languages, in CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS) — never a second regeneration, because a validator/regenerator loop is exactly how the model finds new vocabulary for the same assertion. Fields with no fallback (a signal item's claim, a still_worth_verifying question, a sources_of_noise field, a person-specific item) are blanked so the structural filter drops the item. 5b: a signal item whose basis fell back gets its CLAIM re-judged alone and dropped unless it passes — a fixed basis under an unlicensed claim would lend it the very logical veneer the pipeline removes. WHY: five consecutive prompt-only passes (tool rules 14/27-29, then two rounds of the global epistemics contract) all failed the same live nutrition test the same way — the model stopped saying 'research shows' and started stating bare or hedged premises ('hormones regulate appetite and energy expenditure', 'meal timing may interact with circadian rhythms', 'intermittent fasting is a workable structure for some people'), or laundering them through 'this follows from the accounting relationship'. No lexical marker exists for that; a phrase list structurally cannot see it. MEASURED DURING BUILD: (a) judge recall collapses with batch size — one call over all 48 fields flagged 3 and missed the two plainest violations; the same two fields alone were both flagged in 1.7s — hence SEMANTIC_BATCH_SIZE=6, parallel; (b) the judge is consistent (3/3) on what it flags but neighborhood-sensitive, hence two offset passes unioned at stage 2; (c) the judge itself got laundered by 'this follows from the structure...' framing until told to judge every sentence on its own. Standalone replay of a leaked response through the finished pipeline: semantic=9 rewritten=6 fallback=2 blanked=1, and a fresh judge pass over the result found the flagship leaks gone. Live: 4 consecutive runs, fallbacks firing 1-5 times per run, route time ~60s (parallel judge calls; +10-20s vs v6). COST: roughly 20-35 small MODELS.SMART calls per request on a leaky response — a deliberate trade for a tool whose entire promise is this discipline. GOLDEN: schema unchanged; sources_of_noise and what_general_claims_cant_decide are now optionalSections on every case because the pipeline legitimately empties them (their fields have no fallback text, so a flagged item drops). DO NOT: collapse the judge back to one big batch; add a second regeneration attempt; let a rewrite through when its recheck was unavailable; give sources_of_noise/still_worth_verifying fields a fallback (they'd become filler).
_meta.v7_1_note: V7.1 (same day): SEMANTIC_CHECK_SYSTEM is now the owner's supplied validation prompt (PASS only if every substantive claim is visitor-supplied or logical analysis needing no extra real-world premise; FAIL on remembered knowledge, unsupplied examples, 'unestablished then asserted anyway', hedge-disguised claims, conclusions not established by validated material; counterfactual key test), wrapped in the batch/JSON contract plus a CLARIFICATIONS block. Measured: as written it over-flagged the tool's own correct output (flagged 'is an empirical question this analysis cannot settle'; one live run blanked the whole Signal section). Restoring the owner's earlier 'ignore statements that merely define / analyze wording / identify missing info / say evidence is needed' list fixed that (replay: blanked 1 -> 0, signal item kept). Live cost with the final prompt on the nutrition scenario: 12 fallbacks in one run (5/8 bottom-line items boilerplate) — the rule applied faithfully; boilerplate density is the owner's call, documented in the tool notes. Flagship BAD sentences ('hormonal factors operate within the energy-balance relationship', 'not competing explanations — they interact') added verbatim to MUST-fail examples after the solo re-judge passed one of them once.
_meta.v7_2_note: V7.2 (same day): fallback PRESENTATION only, judge untouched. (1) bottom_line fallback split into per-list wording takeaway/skeptical/would_help, each with a _many variant, 13 languages. (2) optional sub-fields (kernel_of_truth, signal limits) are OMITTED on failure (null) instead of replaced — UI renders them only when present. (3) collapseBottomLineFallbacks: within each bottom-line list, survivors untouched, all fallback items fold into at most one bullet placed last (singular wording for one failure, _many for several) — a variable-length Bottom Line, per DEFTBRAIN_OUTPUT_STANDARD_V2's preference for omission over redundant completeness. Bug caught by the fallback unit test before shipping: English would_help fallbacks began 'Evidence about…', matching CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, so the structural filter would have dropped the collapsed bullet; reworded. Live run 7: one collapsed takeaway bullet, kernels 3/4 (one omitted), no repeated fallbacks.
_meta.v8_note: V8 (2026-09-11): owner-supplied rebuild replaces the source-free claim-analysis architecture (V4-V7.2) with research-first: lib/claimResearch.js runs a bounded Anthropic web_search pre-pass through groundedFacts (maxUses default 6 for this tool, 3 everywhere else), returns a structured evidence packet, and the synthesis call (no tools) may make empirical claims ONLY from the packet with source_ids validated in code. New response fields: analysis_mode='verified_research', research_status, researched_at, sources_examined[{id,title,publisher,url,date,source_type}] (pruned to sources actually cited), and source_ids[] on the_signal items / the_noise items / still_worth_verifying items. Cold cache: waits up to SIGNAL_RESEARCH_COLD_WAIT_MS then returns HTTP 503 code:research_unavailable rather than an unresearched answer — so a golden re-run can 503 on a cold server; run the case once to warm (24h TTL), then check. the_noise is now optional (items without a surviving source id drop). The regex/judge/rewrite/fallback machinery and CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS are gone; earlier DO-NOT notes in SIGNALVSNOISE-NOTES.md V4-V7.2 are superseded, not reversed. See the V8 section there for kit findings.
_meta.v8_3_note: V8.3 (2026-09-11): speed. (1) synthesis split into two parallel disjoint-key calls (signal+noise 3000 tok / verify+cant-decide+bottom-line+sources-of-noise 2200 tok) — same packet, different schema halves; (2) hard word caps per field in the prompt; (3) two-phase UX: new POST /signal-vs-noise/research returns immediately ({status:'pending', sources:[]} 202 while the fetch runs, {status:'ready', researched_at, claim_count, sources} once cached — starts the fetch on a cold topic; own rate-limit bucket 20/min), the client polls it every ~6s untracked (pollToolEndpoint), shows 'N sources found', then calls the main endpoint which finds the research cached and runs synthesis only. Main endpoint unchanged for direct callers (60s cold wait, 503). New golden case research-status-investing-warm checks the readiness shape; sources optional because a cold server answers pending.
_meta.v9_note: V9 (2026-10-27): owner's review. Answer restructured to a short verdict then one compact assessment per claim (claims[]: claim, assessment supported|overstated|mixed|unresolved, finding, evidence, limitation, source_ids) — replaces the_signal / the_noise / still_worth_verifying / the_bottom_line / framing. T13 checks (lib/evidenceFit.js; link, date and figure verification in claimResearch). Cases now use the built-in examples (exampleId) so their research is the stored seed: a golden run pays for synthesis and checks only.

input.conflictingAdvice: Index funds always win vs. active management can beat the market, time in market beats timing the market vs. valuations matter, real estate vs. stocks

output.topic_as_understood: Whether index funds reliably beat active management, whether staying invested outperforms market timing, whether valuations predict returns, and whether real estate or stocks produce better long-term returns
output.verdict: Index funds' structural advantage over active management is well-documented but not absolute across all categories. Staying invested and valuations both matter — they create genuine tension rather than contradiction. The real estate vs. stocks comparison remains mixed, shaped heavily by what costs and income streams you include and which time period you examine.
what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether your specific time horizon, tax situation, and liquidity needs favor real estate, stocks, or a mix
Whether your starting point today — given current valuations — changes how much the 'stay invested' guidance applies to you
Whether any active fund you are considering falls in the minority that has historically outperformed net of fees

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A finding that holds across most cases or long periods gets restated as 'always' or 'never,' erasing the exceptions the data actually shows
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Universal language — 'always wins,' 'always beats' — where the underlying data reports percentages or averages, not universals

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: One figure includes rental income and the other does not, making direct comparison misleading about which asset class actually performed better.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A return figure for real estate that omits rental income, leverage, maintenance, and transaction costs while the stock figure includes dividends

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A 10-year comparison and a 145-year comparison can reach opposite conclusions about which asset class won — the period chosen determines the answer.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A comparison that leads with a specific 10- or 30-year window without acknowledging that a different window reverses or closes the gap

claims.claim: Index funds always beat active management
claims.finding: In 2025, 79% of active large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed the S&P 500 net of fees, and underperformance rates generally rose as time horizons lengthened — but 'always' is not supported: active managers have outperformed in specific categories and years.
claims.evidence: SPIVA U.S. Scorecard, S&P Dow Jones Indices, 25-year dataset through year-end 2025
claims.limitation: SPIVA data is net of fees, so manager skill and cost drag are not separable; fee structure is a structural headwind in the data.

claims.claim: Time in the market beats timing the market
claims.finding: Research reports that missing the 10 best market days over 35 years roughly halved returns, while immediate investment captured about 92% of theoretically perfect timing gains. Bank of America historical data showed that staying invested for 15 years in U.S. equities eliminated the likelihood of negative returns. These findings come from secondary sources only and describe historical patterns; they do not establish that future equity markets will continue to produce positive long-run returns.
claims.evidence: Schwab research summarized by Yahoo Finance; Schroders data and Bank of America data summarized by Tribe Impact Capital — all secondary only
claims.limitation: Only secondary sources were found for this claim; the historical pattern holds for broadly diversified index portfolios but does not necessarily apply to individual securities or illiquid assets.

claims.finding: Research across 16–17 international equity markets found a consistent negative relationship between the CAPE ratio and subsequent 10-to-20-year real stock returns: higher starting valuations predicted lower long-run returns.
claims.evidence: Campbell and Shiller (1988) and follow-on international studies, reviewed in an SSRN working paper (Keimling, 2016)
claims.limitation: CAPE predicts long-run averages with meaningful but imperfect accuracy; it is a poor short- or medium-term timing tool, and high CAPE can persist for years without correction.

claims.claim: Real estate produces better long-term returns than stocks
claims.finding: Over a 30-year period ending April 2025, the S&P 500 returned about 10.29% annually versus about 8.78% for real estate by one measure; a 145-year multi-country study found near-identical inflation-adjusted returns when rental income is included. REITs (which capture rental income) have been broadly competitive with the S&P 500 over 30 years.
claims.evidence: Morningstar Direct data via CNBC (2025); BiggerPockets summary of Jorda et al., Quarterly Journal of Economics (2019); NAREIT data via AskDoss (2026) — all secondary sources
claims.limitation: Direct comparisons are structurally unreliable: stock returns are typically total-return figures while real estate comparisons often exclude rental income, leverage, maintenance costs, and ~6% transaction costs; the 'better' conclusion shifts substantially depending on period and method.

claims.claim: Stocks produce better long-term returns than real estate
claims.finding: The stock-outperformance case and the real estate case draw on the same data and the same period — the findings are summarized in the real estate finding above. What shifts here is framing: stock outperformance is clearest in the recent 30-year window; near-parity appears over the 145-year horizon when rental income is included on the real estate side.
claims.evidence: Same sources as the real estate finding above.
claims.limitation: Same structural comparison problems apply; time period chosen is the primary driver of which side appears to win.

sources_examined.title: U.S. Persistence Scorecard Year-End 2025
sources_examined.publisher: S&P Global / S&P Dow Jones Indices (SPIVA)

sources_examined.title: Predicting Stock Market Returns Using the Shiller CAPE — An Improvement Towards Traditional Value Indicators? (SSRN abstract)
Real Estate vs. Stocks (What 145 Years of Returns Tells Us) — summarizing Jorda et al., 'The Rate of Return on Everything, 1870–2015,' Quarterly Journal of Economics 2019
Real estate and gold vs. stocks: Best long-term investment
Real Estate vs. S&P 500: Historical Returns, Risk, and Cost Comparison
Real Estate vs Stocks: Full Comparison

input.conflictingAdvice: Indexfonds gewinnen immer vs. aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen, Zeit im Markt schlägt das Timing vs. Bewertungen zählen, Immobilien vs. Aktien

output.topic_as_understood: Welche Anlagestrategien sind empirisch belegt: Indexfonds vs. aktives Management, Zeit im Markt vs. Timing, Immobilien vs. Aktien
output.verdict: Indexfonds schlagen aktive Fonds in der Mehrheit der gemessenen Fälle, besonders über lange Zeiträume – aber nicht immer und überall. Bewertungen zum Einstiegszeitpunkt beeinflussen die langfristigen Renditen nachweislich: höheres CAPE zum Einstieg geht historisch mit niedrigeren späteren Langfristrenditen einher. Ob und wie stark das den Vorteil des frühen Investierens aufwiegt, lässt die vorliegende Evidenz offen. Immobilien gegen Aktien bleibt strukturell schwer vergleichbar; die verfügbaren Daten lassen keine klare Überlegenheit einer Seite erkennen.
what_general_claims_cant_decide: Welcher Anteil des eigenen Vermögens in Aktien, Immobilien oder beides sinnvoll ist, hängt von persönlicher Risikobereitschaft, Zeithorizont und Liquiditätsbedarf ab – das liefert die allgemeine Evidenz nicht.
Ob der aktuelle Einstiegszeitpunkt bei hohen CAPE-Werten das eigene Renditeziel gefährdet, lässt sich ohne Angaben zur geplanten Haltedauer und zum konkreten Portfolio nicht beurteilen.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Aus 'trifft auf die Mehrheit der Fälle zu' wird 'gilt immer' – Ausnahmen nach Kategorie, Zeitraum oder Markt verschwinden.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Formulierungen ohne Einschränkung: 'immer', 'nie', 'schlägt stets' – ohne Angabe von Zeitraum oder Kategorie.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Aktienrenditen werden als Gesamtrendite (Kurs plus Dividenden) gemessen, Immobilien oft nur als Preisentwicklung ohne Mieteinnahmen, Transaktionskosten oder Hebel – das macht den Vergleich strukturell ungleich.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Vergleiche ohne explizite Angabe, ob Mietrendite, Instandhaltungskosten und Fremdkapital eingerechnet sind.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Studien, die von Anbietern einer bestimmten Anlageklasse veröffentlicht werden, können methodische Schwächen aufweisen oder selektiv präsentierte Ergebnisse enthalten – unabhängige Überprüfung ist schwer zu erkennen.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Studie stammt vom Anbieter eines Produkts, das von der Schlussfolgerung direkt profitiert, ohne unabhängige Überprüfung.

claims.finding: Im Jahr 2025 schnitten 79 % der aktiv verwalteten US-Large-Cap-Fonds schlechter ab als der S&P 500 – das viertschwächste Ergebnis in 25 Jahren SPIVA-Daten. Underperformance stieg mit längeren Zeithorizonten, aber 'immer' gilt nicht für alle Kategorien und Zeiträume.
claims.evidence: SPIVA-Scorecard (S&P Global / S&P Dow Jones Indices), 25-Jahres-Reihe bis 2025
claims.limitation: In bestimmten Kategorien (z. B. Small-Caps, ausgewählte Anleihen) schlugen aktive Manager in einzelnen Jahren ihre Benchmarks – das 'immer' ist nicht gedeckt.

claims.claim: Aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen
claims.finding: Ergänzend zum ersten Befund: Die SPIVA-Daten zeigen außerdem, dass sich Kostenbelastung und Managerfähigkeit nicht vollständig trennen lassen – Underperformance liegt also teils an Gebühren, nicht ausschließlich am Stock-Picking.
claims.evidence: SPIVA-Scorecard (S&P Global / S&P Dow Jones Indices), 25-Jahres-Reihe
claims.limitation: Kostenbelastung und Managerfähigkeit lassen sich in den SPIVA-Daten nicht vollständig trennen – die Schwäche liegt also teils bei Gebühren, nicht nur beim Stock-Picking.

claims.claim: Zeit im Markt schlägt das Timing
claims.finding: Sekundärquellen dokumentieren Szenarien, in denen sofortiges Investieren einen hohen Anteil der Gewinne von perfektem Market-Timing erreicht und in denen das Verpassen einzelner starker Handelstage über längere Zeiträume erhebliche Auswirkungen hatte. Primäre Forschung zu diesen Befunden ist in diesem Paket nicht enthalten.
claims.evidence: Schwab-Analyse (via Yahoo Finance, S2); Schroders-Daten und Bank-of-America-Daten (via Tribe Impact Capital, S3) – nur Sekundärquellen
claims.limitation: Nur Sekundärquellen gefunden; das Paket enthält keine primäre oder institutionelle Studie, die diesen Befund direkt belegt.

claims.finding: Forschung über 16–17 internationale Aktienmärkte zeigt einen konsistenten negativen Zusammenhang zwischen dem CAPE-Verhältnis und den realen Aktienrenditen über 10–20 Jahre: höheres CAPE zum Einstiegszeitpunkt geht mit niedrigeren späteren Renditen einher.
claims.evidence: Campbell & Shiller (1988) und Folgestudien, zusammengefasst in einem SSRN-Preprint (Keimling, 2016), S4
claims.limitation: CAPE ist ein schlechtes Timing-Instrument für kurze Zeiträume und kann über Jahre erhöht bleiben, ohne dass eine Korrektur folgt.

claims.finding: Jorda et al. (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019) berichten über 16 Länder im Zeitraum 1870–2015 nahezu identische inflationsbereinigte Gesamtrenditen für Wohnimmobilien (einschließlich Mieteinnahmen) und Aktien – die konkreten Prozentzahlen aus dieser Studie konnten anhand der vorliegenden Quelle nicht verifiziert werden. Über andere Zeitfenster hinweg zeigen sich unterschiedliche Ergebnisse: Morningstar-Daten der 30 Jahre bis April 2025 weisen einen Vorsprung für den S&P 500 (10,29 % p.a.) gegenüber Immobilien (8,78 % p.a.) aus. Von 1992 bis 2024 erzielte der S&P 500 etwa 10,39 % durchschnittliche jährliche Renditen, während die Immobilienpreissteigerung ohne Mieteinnahmen etwa 5,5 % betrug. REITs (die Mieteinnahmen einbeziehen) erzielten laut NAREIT-Daten ungefähr 10–12 % jährlich über die letzten 30 Jahre – in einer Größenordnung, die mit dem S&P 500 vergleichbar ist.
claims.evidence: Jorda et al., The Rate of Return on Everything, 1870–2015 (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019); Morningstar-Daten via CNBC (S6); NAREIT-Daten via AskDoss (S7); S&P 500-Daten via Wealth Formula (S8)
claims.limitation: Direktvergleiche sind strukturell schwierig: Aktien werden als Gesamtrendite gemessen, Immobilien oft nur als Preissteigerung ohne Mieteinnahmen, Hebeleffekte, Transaktionskosten und Instandhaltung. Das gewählte Zeitfenster verändert das Ergebnis erheblich.

input.conflictingAdvice: Screen time is destroying kids vs. it depends on content, tiger parenting vs. free-range, homework helps vs. homework is harmful

output.topic_as_understood: Whether screen time uniformly harms children, whether tiger parenting outperforms free-range approaches, and whether homework helps or hurts kids academically
output.verdict: Screen time effects depend substantially on content type and viewing context rather than total time alone. Tiger parenting was associated with lower academic outcomes compared to supportive parenting in a longitudinal study of Chinese-American families, but generalizability to other cultural groups is unclear. Homework shows a small positive association with academic achievement, larger at secondary than elementary levels; parental involvement specifically shows a weak negative association, likely because parents help more when children struggle. Genuine uncertainty remains about how these patterns extend across different populations and individual circumstances.
what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether the research findings apply to a specific child depends on details not supplied here: the child's age and grade level, what content or type of homework is involved, whether a parent's circumstance matches the study populations, and individual characteristics that moderate outcomes.
How homework's modest benefit or potential stress varies by the specific grade level, subject, and type of assignment involved.
Whether a given parenting approach fits a particular child — the population patterns in the findings above do not determine individual fit.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Total screen time or homework quantity gets reported as the key factor, while content type, grade level, and context — which the evidence shows matter substantially — drop out of popular summaries.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Claims state a flat rule ('X hours is too much') with no mention of what the child is watching or what grade they are in.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Observational associations between a parenting style or habit and an outcome get restated as proof that one causes the other, even when reverse causation is a documented alternative explanation.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Look for 'leads to' or 'causes' where the underlying study design was observational or cross-sectional, not experimental.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Popular labels like 'tiger' or 'free-range' get treated as well-defined research categories, when the empirical literature uses different profiles — and evidence for or against one label is applied to the other without a direct comparison.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A source claims research proves 'free-range is better' without citing studies that directly compared free-range to other approaches.

claims.finding: Content type and viewing context — not total screen time alone — drive outcomes. non-child-directed content and age-inappropriate content were associated with worse cognitive and psychosocial outcomes.
claims.evidence: 2024 JAMA Pediatrics systematic review and meta-analysis (S1); 2024 JAMA Pediatrics cohort study of 15,965 kindergartners (S2); 2025 Frontiers in Developmental Psychology scoping review of children aged 0–36 months (S3)
claims.limitation: Most research is observational; children with developmental difficulties may consume more or different content, making causal direction difficult to establish.

claims.finding: In a longitudinal study tracking 444 Chinese-American families over eight years, children with tiger parents had lower GPA, more depressive symptoms, greater alienation, and lower educational attainment than children with supportive parents.
claims.evidence: APA Division 7 professional body summary (S4); primary study hosted on ResearchGate, 2023 (S5)
claims.limitation: Research focuses heavily on Chinese-American samples; whether findings generalize to other cultural groups is unclear, and parenting behaviors may carry different meaning across contexts.

claims.finding: The research found here assessed tiger and supportive parenting approaches directly, but did not include direct controlled studies of free-range parenting as a defined category. Positive claims about free-range approaches rest on research documenting harms of over-protective parenting rather than trials of free-range methods specifically.
claims.limitation: Only secondary-level support was found for free-range parenting claims; direct evidence was absent from the research found here.

claims.finding: Two meta-analyses found positive associations between homework and academic achievement, but effect sizes were small (d = 0.229 in one; moderate time associated with higher scores in another) and substantially larger at secondary than elementary levels, suggesting the benefit is real but modest and grade-dependent.
claims.evidence: Meta-analytic review in Issues in Educational Research, 2017 (S6); meta-analysis using TIMSS data, Psicologia Educativa, 2022 (S7)
claims.limitation: Most research measures homework quantity, not quality; effects vary substantially by grade level, subject, and homework type.

claims.finding: The achievement literature does not consistently support a harm finding. However, parental homework involvement specifically showed a weak negative association with achievement (r = -0.064 across 378,222 participants in one meta-analysis; students receiving more help had lower achievement, d = 0.23, in a PISA meta-analysis) — most likely reflecting that parents help more when children already struggle, not that help itself causes harm.
claims.evidence: Three-level meta-analysis of 28 studies (378,222 participants), 2024 (S9); meta-analysis of 180 effects using PISA data, PubMed, 2022 (S8)
claims.limitation: Achievement meta-analyses generally do not measure stress or well-being, so excess or poorly designed homework may carry costs the academic literature does not capture.

input.conflictingAdvice: Sleep 8 hours vs. polyphasic sleep, phone before bed ruins sleep vs. blue light glasses fix it, sleep debt is real vs. you can't catch up

output.topic_as_understood: Whether adults need exactly 8 hours of sleep, whether polyphasic schedules are a viable alternative, whether phone use before bed harms sleep via blue light, and whether sleep debt can be recovered
output.verdict: The 8-hour target is a simplification of a 7–9 hour evidence-based range; polyphasic sleep beyond naps shows adverse outcomes in the available research; blue light is only part of why phones disrupt sleep, and blue-light glasses show little benefit in trials; sleep debt recovery is partial and outcome-dependent.
what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether your own sleep need falls at the short or long end of the 7-9 hour range — individual variation exists and the general evidence cannot establish it for you.
Whether your specific pre-bed phone habits are driving your sleep problems, or whether content, timing, and arousal are bigger factors than the light itself.
How much of your personal sleep debt, if any, is recoverable — the answer depends on how chronic and severe the deficit is, which the general evidence does not determine.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A range like 7-9 hours collapses into a single memorable target — '8 hours' — that is easier to repeat but narrower than the evidence supports.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A sleep recommendation stated as one exact number with no mention of individual variation or age-based differences.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Establishing that blue light can affect melatonin gets extended into the claim that blocking it with glasses fixes sleep, skipping evidence that glasses may not replicate the effect.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A product or behavior is promoted on the basis of a plausible mechanism, without citing trials of the product itself.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Both 'sleep debt is real' and 'you can't catch up' are each partly supported, so either side can quote evidence selectively while ignoring the outcome-dependent nuance the research shows.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A claim about sleep recovery states a flat yes or no without specifying which outcomes recover and how quickly.

claims.finding: A fixed 8-hour target is not what the evidence supports; a 2025 systematic review of 133 meta-analyses found 7–9 hours appropriate for adults 26–64, and 7–8 hours for adults 65+. Sleeping beyond 8–9 hours was associated with elevated mortality risk in one large meta-analysis, though long sleep also serves as a marker of underlying illness.
claims.evidence: NSF 2025 systematic review (133 meta-analyses); 2020 overview of systematic reviews; NSF 2015 final recommendations report
claims.limitation: Most large studies are observational, so a causal link between sleep duration and health outcomes cannot be firmly established.

claims.claim: Polyphasic sleep is a viable alternative
claims.finding: An NSF consensus panel screening over 40,000 publications found no evidence of benefit from polyphasic schedules (excluding naps and siestas), and multiple studies showed worse mood, cognitive performance, and memory recall on such schedules. A controlled study also found strongly decreased growth hormone and a 90% dropout rate.
claims.evidence: NSF consensus panel review (22 retained papers from 40,672 screened), 2021; controlled polyphasic sleep study, bioRxiv preprint, 2023
claims.limitation: The NSF review excluded nap and siesta schedules; biphasic sleep with a single daytime nap has a distinct and less-studied evidence profile than extreme multi-nap schedules. The controlled study is a preprint.

claims.finding: Light-emitting devices before bed have been associated with delayed melatonin onset and impaired next-morning alertness in experimental studies. However, screen use involves multiple mechanisms—psychological arousal, engaging content, deferred sleep timing—that are difficult to separate from light exposure alone.
claims.evidence: 2024 primary study in Chronobiology in Medicine on blue light and circadian disruption in adolescent and young adult students [S7]
claims.limitation: Most experimental studies use controlled conditions that may not match typical real-world phone use, so the size of the effect in ordinary settings is unclear.

claims.finding: A 2023 Cochrane systematic review of 17 RCTs found that blue-light filtering spectacles make little difference to sleep quality, with evidence for sleep outcomes characterized as indeterminate.
claims.evidence: Cochrane systematic review of 17 RCTs, 2023
claims.limitation: The available RCT evidence does not establish whether effects differ for specific populations such as shift workers, insomniacs, or those with jet lag — the general adult findings may not extend to them.

claims.finding: A 2025 systematic review found sleep debt is real in the sense that chronic deprivation produces measurable impairments; weekend catch-up sleep provides partial short-term recovery of mood, fatigue, and some cognitive performance, but cannot fully reverse the effects of chronic deprivation.
claims.evidence: 2025 systematic review in Sleep and Breathing (Springer Nature / PubMed)
claims.limitation: Weekend catch-up also shifts circadian timing later, potentially creating 'social jet lag' that compounds impairment at the start of the following week.

claims.claim: You can't catch up on lost sleep
claims.finding: Recovery is outcome-dependent: basic alertness and reaction time recover relatively quickly, while metabolic and higher-order cognitive outcomes recover more slowly and incompletely. A small acute deficit may be substantially reversed; weeks of restriction appear harder to repair with two days of extra sleep.
claims.evidence: Same source as cited for the finding above.
claims.limitation: Most studies involve controlled laboratory conditions or specific populations, limiting how far findings extend to varied real-world sleep patterns.
